title: Tired With a Big Liver and Spleen / Nodes Point to the Blood, Not the Liver

blocks.text: Tired With a Big Liver and Spleen / Nodes Point to the Blood, Not the Liver

AMaC MRCP PACES · R2-07 · Physical examination · PACES Station 4, abdominal examination encounter · Skills A, B, D, E, G · 10 min: up to 6 min examining, then at least 4 min of examiner questions · Guidelines: NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (published 23 June 2015; last updated 15 April 2026) · Related AMaC: Abdominal examination: splenomegaly; chronic liver disease

Mr Alan Prowse, 68, a retired electrician, has felt tired for four months and has noticed a fullness under his ribs. Please examine his abdomen to establish the cause. You have up to 6 minutes to examine, followed by questions.

sections.heading: 4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap

blocks.text: The Hook. Both liver and spleen enlarged, with generalised nodes and no stigmata of chronic liver disease, is most likely a blood problem; look for the nodes before you commit.

The Examiner Trap. Candidates find both organs and announce portal hypertension, then never examine the neck, armpits or groins. Pass: after finding both organs, look for nodes and for liver stigmata before naming a cause. Fail: a liver diagnosis with no nodes examined.

rows: Think
Say
Do
Both organs are enlarged: liver disease or blood disease?
"Mr Prowse, may I examine your tummy? Tell me if anything is sore."
Introduce, consent, ask about pain, lie flat, expose, look; hands, eyes, chest; start in the right iliac fossa.
Separate liver from spleen; look for fluid and kidneys.
"I can feel the liver edge and the spleen. I'll check for fluid and the kidneys."
Liver edge, spleen notch, dull, cannot get above it; ballot kidneys; shifting dullness.
Nodes versus liver stigmata decide the cause.
"I'd like to examine your neck, armpits and groins, and look for signs of liver disease."
Cervical, axillary, inguinal nodes; spider naevi, jaundice, palmar erythema, bruising, pallor; JVP.
Name the likely cause and the first blood test.
"This looks haematological, such as lymphoma or a chronic leukaemia. I'd arrange a blood count and film."
Cover him, thank him; present findings, differential, urgent blood count, haematology referral.

blocks.text: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. High-performance includes the pass behaviours. This station-specific grid is an AMaC teaching framework mapped to PACES skills, not an official mark scheme. Consent, hand hygiene, dignity and an appropriate chaperone are baseline professional practice.
Not used for this station type: the patient is a real or simulated patient and the findings are in section 8.

Findings (released as each step is done). Temperature 36.8°C, pulse 84, BP 132/78 (scenario values). Mild pallor; small forearm bruises; no jaundice, spider naevi, palmar erythema or asterixis. Liver edge 4 cm below the right costal margin, firm, non-tender. Spleen 5 cm below the left costal margin, notch felt, cannot get above it. Kidneys not ballotable; no ascites. Generalised rubbery, non-tender nodes: neck, armpits, groins. JVP not raised; no oedema.

Question ladder. Q1 Findings and diagnosis (R4, R5): hepatosplenomegaly with generalised lymphadenopathy; lymphoproliferative disorder. Q2 Alternatives (R5): lymphoma, chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, myeloproliferative disease; portal hypertension, infection, infiltration. Q3 Investigations (R6): blood count and film, liver tests, LDH, viral serology, CT, tissue diagnosis. Q4 Referral (R7): very urgent full blood count within 48 hours; urgent suspected cancer referral (NICE NG12). Q5 Safety net (R7): fever, bleeding, drenching sweats need urgent assessment.

Normal-findings variant for a separate teaching exercise. No organomegaly, nodes or stigmata. The candidate must say the abdomen is normal and suggest causes of tiredness. Do not switch the defined case to this variant during the encounter.
Curveball 1. "He is feverish." Safe: urgent senior review for infection or low counts.
Curveball 2. "Heart failure?" Safe: congestion enlarges the liver, but the JVP is normal and the spleen is large.

Fail performance
(Lifts his shirt and presses into the left upper abdomen without asking. [R1 Fail] [R2 Fail] Does not examine the neck or groins. [R3 Fail])
CANDIDATE: He has ascites and spider naevi. [R4 Fail] This is chronic liver disease with portal hypertension. [R5 Fail]
EXAMINER: What would you do next?
CANDIDATE: A liver ultrasound. [R6 Fail] I'd see him again in the routine clinic. [R7 Fail]
Examiner note: No consent or pain question, absent signs reported, no nodes examined, and a liver diagnosis the findings do not support. Routine follow-up leaves a possible blood cancer unexplored.
Pass performance
CANDIDATE: Hello Mr Prowse, I'm going to examine your tummy. Is that all right? Is it sore anywhere? Tell me if anything hurts. [R1 Pass]
(Cleans his hands, lies him flat, looks at hands and eyes, palpates from the right iliac fossa upwards with his breathing, percusses and checks for ascites. [R2 Pass])
(Examines the neck, armpits and groins, and looks for liver stigmata. [R3 Pass])
CANDIDATE: Thank you, Mr Prowse. I'll cover you now. [R1 Pass]
CANDIDATE: He has a firm enlarged liver, a large spleen and generalised rubbery nodes, with no jaundice or spider naevi. [R4 Pass]
CANDIDATE: This looks like a lymphoproliferative problem, such as lymphoma or a chronic leukaemia. [R5 Pass]
EXAMINER: How would you investigate?
CANDIDATE: A full blood count and film, liver tests and clotting. [R6 Pass]
EXAMINER: And what next?
CANDIDATE: A very urgent full blood count within 48 hours and an urgent suspected cancer referral to haematology. [R7 Pass]
Examiner note: Safe, complete and in order. Did not name alternatives, give sizes or offer a safety net.
High-performance performance
CANDIDATE: Hello Mr Prowse, I'm going to examine your tummy. Is that all right? Is it sore anywhere? Tell me if anything hurts. [R1 High]
(Lies him flat, looks at hands and eyes, palpates from the right iliac fossa upwards with his breathing, percusses and checks for ascites. [R2 High])
CANDIDATE: Mr Prowse, may I offer a chaperone? I'll tell you what I'm doing; please say if anything is tender. [R1 High]
(Starts in the right iliac fossa, feels the splenic notch, shows he cannot get above the spleen, and ballots both kidneys. [R2 High])
(Checks neck, armpits and groins in order, then looks for bruising, pallor, jaundice and the JVP. [R3 High])

CANDIDATE: The liver edge is 4 cm down, firm and non-tender; the spleen is 5 cm down. There are rubbery nodes in the neck, armpits and groins, mild pallor and forearm bruises. No ascites, jaundice or raised JVP. [R4 High]
CANDIDATE: This is most likely a blood cause. Liver disease is less likely without stigmata or ascites; infection and infiltration are other options. [R5 High]
EXAMINER: How would you investigate?
CANDIDATE: A blood count and film, liver tests, LDH, viral serology and a CT scan, with a tissue diagnosis through haematology. [R6 High]
EXAMINER: And what would you tell him?
CANDIDATE: Why I want the blood count very urgently, that I'm referring him urgently under the suspected cancer pathway, and to come back at once with fever, bleeding or drenching sweats. [R7 High]
CANDIDATE: Thank you for letting me examine you. [R1 High]
Examiner note: Separated blood from liver causes with reasons and gave a safety net.
R3: Stopping at the abdomen misses the generalised nodes that point to a blood cause; the liver label then goes unchallenged.
R4: Reporting ascites or spider naevi that are absent shows that signs were assumed, not found.
R5: Naming chronic liver disease with no stigmata and no ascites ignores the nodes and sends the work-up the wrong way.
R7: Routine follow-up for hepatosplenomegaly with nodes delays diagnosis of a possible blood cancer.
R1: Palpating without consent or an offer to stop is a welfare failure whatever else is found.
"Let me look for nodes before I decide."
"No stigmata and no ascites, so I doubt a liver cause."
"I'd start with a blood count and film."
Hepatosplenomegaly with generalised nodes and no liver stigmata points to a blood cause: lymphoma, chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, myeloproliferative disease.
Spleen: notch, dull to percussion, moves with breathing, you cannot get above it, not ballotable.
Portal hypertension gives splenomegaly with ascites and stigmata of chronic liver disease.

NICE NG12 (published 23 June 2015; last updated 15 April 2026): consider a very urgent full blood count for adults with hepatosplenomegaly or generalised lymphadenopathy, and a suspected cancer pathway referral for unexplained lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly.

Generalised lymphadenopathy with hepatosplenomegaly raises concern for a lymphoproliferative disorder, but absent liver stigmata does not exclude liver disease. Arrange the blood count within 48 hours and the suspected cancer referral in parallel; clinical deterioration or significant cytopenias requires more urgent assessment.
THINK: Low blood counts: infection and bleeding.
SAY: "Both organs and nodes: a blood cause first, then prove it."
DO: Consent and pain; nodes; liver stigmata.
NUMBERS: Liver 4 cm, spleen 5 cm below costal margins (scenario values).
TRAP: Calling it chronic liver disease.
FINISH: Blood count and film; urgent suspected cancer referral (NICE NG12).
